items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: And there was one — Charles — what is his name — one of the great white Civil Rights lawyers had written about how he grew up in Texas

ctx.x: I don’t think a lot of people listen to New Orleans music anymore. It’s too bad because it’s still great music. There was a lot of brilliance in the 1920s and coming forward. And it still speaks, at least to me today. Louis Armstrong for example, was a voice for the

ages. I mean I don’t think he will ever be obsolete. But still I think most people know Louis from the singing he did say during the 1950s to the end of his life than they do from the times when he was breaking through and establishing himself as the future of music. And there was one — Charles — what is his name — one of the great white Civil Rights lawyers had written about how he grew up in Texas in a world of segregation and had assumed all of the things that go with segregation and Jim Crow about…

I had the good fortune to interview the trombone player Benny Powell. And he said in his opinion no great art ever came from happiness — that there had to be adversity for, he said “great art to be formed.” And I wonder how you feel about that?
